knowledge_type_note: A tactical motif rather than a strategic principle: it is a concrete forcing sequence whose correctness is settled by calculation, not judgement. It happens to occur in pawn structures, which is why it is often taught as strategy.

history.notes: The pattern is old and anonymous; it appears in endgame manuals long before any of the sources consulted here. No coiner is claimed and none was found.

engine_era_note: Wholly concrete, so engines settle it exactly. Nothing about the concept has been revised; what engines add is that the boundary conditions — how advanced the pawns must be, how far the king may stand — can now be checked in seconds rather than analysed.

preconditions: Opposing pawn groups face each other with no passer for either side
The attacker has at least as many pawns in the group and they are advanced
A pawn advance creates two levers simultaneously
indicators_for: A trio against a trio, the attacker's one rank further on
The defending king is outside the square of the prospective passer
The attacker has a space advantage in that pawn group
Whichever way the defender captures, a different pawn gets through
indicators_against: The defending king is close enough to catch the runner — check the rule of the square first
The attacking pawns are too far back; the same structure one rank earlier usually fails outright
The defender can decline the capture and hold
The attacker's own king is needed elsewhere and cannot support
false_positive_traps: A pawn sacrifice that creates a passer is not a breakthrough unless the passer actually cannot be stopped. The rule of the square decides this and is cheap to check.
The pattern is highly recognisable and therefore easy to play on autopilot in a position that is one rank short of it working.

typical_plans: Push the middle pawn to create two levers, then sacrifice again to deflect, then run
Combine with an outside passer to stretch the defending king
Prophylactically: prevent the lever structure from arising at all
typical_moves: b6! in the a5-b5-c5 against a7-b7-c7 structure
g6! and h6! and f6! in the kingside mirror (f5-g5-h5 against f7-g7-h7)
typical_pawn_structures: Trio against trio, one rank apart
typical_piece_arrangements: Typically none — this is usually a pure pawn ending
tactical_consequences: Produces an unstoppable passer by force
strategic_consequences: Makes a space advantage in a pawn group concrete
Turns apparently blocked and drawn endings into wins

exceptions: Fails outright without enough space. Moving the whole structure one rank back is the standard demonstration.
Fails if the defending king is inside the square of the resulting passer.
The defender can sometimes decline the first capture and hold.
limitations: Entirely concrete. It should be verified by calculation every time, not recognised and trusted.

SCOPE, stated rather than hidden: the detector runs only when nothing but kings and pawns is left, because the rule of the square - which the record's own false-positive trap names as the thing that decides - is a proof there and a guess anywhere else. In a middlegame the same pattern may be a breakthrough and this base cannot show that it is, so it says nothing.

It proves that ACCEPTING the offer loses. A defender who declines is answering a different question, and the matcher's wording says so. Over the 788 shipped puzzle positions it fires zero times, which is correct - none of them is a pawn ending - and means the 788 provide no evidence about its false-positive rate.

MEASURED 2026-09-01, and the number is the point. The shipped puzzle generator tags 86 of the 788 positions `pawnBreakthrough`; ZERO of those 86 is a pawn ending, and this base confirms a forced breakthrough in none of them. The two are not measuring the same thing and neither is wrong. The generator's test (tools/puzzle_rules.js) is: the first move is a non-capturing pawn move and after it the destination is winnable by static exchange evaluation OR the pawn is passed - a puzzle classification, which does not ask whether the passer can be stopped. That question is this concept's own registered false-positive trap. The consequence for a later session is that the 788 positions provide no evidence at all about this detector's false-positive rate, and a corpus of pawn endings would have to be built to get any.
misconceptions: That the breakthrough always works in a trio-against-trio structure. Space and king distance decide it.
That it is a strategic idea. It is a forcing tactical sequence that happens to be made of pawns.

examples.note: Constructed test of the canonical trio-versus-trio breakthrough: White a5-b5-c5 against Black a7-b7-c7, kings far away. 1.b6! and whichever way Black captures, a different pawn queens.

engine.verdict_note: A far stronger result than expected. 1.b6! is +64.85 and queens by force. Both alternative first moves LOSE — 1.a6? is -10.25 and 1.c6? is -81.15 — because they let Black break through instead. So the middle pawn is not merely best practice, it is the only move, and the margin over the runner-up is 75 pawns. Settled from depth 3. This is the strongest confirmation in the base that the breakthrough is CONCRETE: order decides everything, and the pattern must be calculated rather than recognised.

examples.note: Wade-Korchnoi, Buenos Aires 1960 (round 10), a5. Human ground truth: the concept is named for this position by Tryfon Gavriel (FM), naming the ply; corroborated by Luke McShane (GM) in The Spectator. Corpus entry `wade-korchnoi-1960-38a5-pawn-breakthrough`, which carries the full annotation, the alternates the annotator rejected, and the engine's verdict. The concept's canonical pattern, in a game, at the moment it decides one. White's a4 and b5 face b6, b7 and c7, and 38.a5 offers a pawn to create two levers at once: 38...bxa5 39.b6! cxb6 40.d6 and the d-pawn runs, because after two captures no black pawn stands on the c-, d- or e-file in front of it and the black king on h5 is four moves from d8 with two moves' work to do. engine.verdict_note: completely, and its variation is the same one. 38.a5 is the engine's first choice at +9.17 against +7.95 for the second, and its principal variation reads a5 bxa5 b6 cxb6 d6 ... d8=Q - the line this base's own detector produced independently. Depth 20 rather than the usual 22+: this is a simplified pawn ending, which the project has already recorded as the case where deep searches stop converging. counterexamples.note: Constructed controlled pair, negative half. IDENTICAL material and identical structure — three pawns against three, kings on the same squares — with White's trio moved one rank back to a4-b4-c4. This isolates the space-advantage condition and nothing else, and it tests pawnbreak.com's testable claim that 'move all pawns one row and the breakthrough does not work at all anymore'.

engine.verdict_note: The claim is confirmed exactly and the margin is enormous. The analogous breakthrough 1.b5 evaluates -5.86 and is NOT best; the quiet 1.a5 at -0.46 is. So the same pattern, with the pawns one rank further back, swings from +64.85 (winning by force) to -5.86 (losing) — a difference of over 70 pawns produced by one rank of space, with material and structure held identical. This is the cleanest confirmation in the base that a positional-sounding precondition can be exactly decisive, and it is why the concept is typed tactical-motif: it must be calculated, never recognised.

by_level.beginner: White gives away two pawns so the third one can run all the way to the end, and the king is too far away to catch it.
by_level.intermediate: A breakthrough. The middle pawn goes first because it attacks two ways at once, so whichever way Black captures, a different pawn gets through.
by_level.advanced: Classic trio breakthrough. Two conditions to check: enough space, and the defending king outside the square of the runner. Both are calculable, so calculate them.
by_level.master: Concrete throughout. Verify both captures, the declined capture, and the full race before playing it — the same pattern one rank back is simply a lost pawn.

by_depth.short: Two pawns are given so the third cannot be stopped.
by_depth.normal: A pawn breakthrough: the middle pawn advances to create two levers at once, a second pawn is sacrificed to deflect the defender, and the third promotes. It works here because the pawns are far enough advanced and the king is outside the square.
by_depth.deep: The canonical form is a5-b5-c5 against a7-b7-c7: 1.b6! and either 1...axb6 2.c6! bxc6 3.a6 or 1...cxb6 2.a6! bxa6 3.c6. The middle pawn leads because it creates two levers, so the defender's choice does not matter. Two conditions decide whether it works and both are concrete — enough space, and the defending king outside the square of the resulting passer. Move the same structure one rank back and it fails entirely, which is why this is a calculation rather than a pattern to trust.

explanations.lesson: When pawns face each other and nothing seems to be happening, check for the breakthrough — and then check the square rule before you play it.

beginner_words: giving up pawns so one can run
avoid: breakthroughs always work in this structure

definition_short: Sacrificing one or two pawns to force through a passer the enemy king cannot catch.
definition_long:
A forcing pawn sacrifice that manufactures a passed pawn out of a blocked structure. The canonical pattern is three pawns against three, one rank apart — white a5, b5, c5 against black a7, b7, c7:

  1.b6! and now
     1...axb6 2.c6! bxc6 3.a6 and the a-pawn queens; or
     1...cxb6 2.a6! bxa6 3.c6 and the c-pawn queens.

The middle pawn moves first because it creates two levers at once, so whichever way the defender captures, another pawn breaks through. The second sacrifice deflects the pawn that would have stopped the runner. Two pawns are given to promote the third.

IT IS CONCRETE, NOT GENERAL. Two conditions decide it and both are calculable. First, SPACE: the attacking pawns must be advanced enough. Move the whole structure one rank back and the breakthrough simply fails — a claim testable directly, and tested in this record. Second, KING DISTANCE: the defending king must be outside the square of the resulting passer, which the rule of the square settles at a glance.

Because both conditions are checkable, a breakthrough should never be played on general grounds. Verify both captures, the refusal to capture, and the full promotion race.
